# Ballard-Rosa, Martin and Scheve (2017): income-tax plans {#sec-br}

@ballard2017structure ask how Americans evaluate federal income-tax schedules. In each of eight
tasks, respondents chose between two tax plans. A plan sets the marginal rate in six income
brackets and states how much revenue it raises compared with current policy, in five categories.
This chapter reproduces the paper's results and figures for this experiment from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: br-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
br <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "br_q4.rds"))
if (is.null(br)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit br_q4.rds; see the installation chapter.")
tab <- function(e, digits = 3) {
  out <- e[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "se", "lower", "upper", "n")]
  out[2:6] <- lapply(out[2:6], round, digits)
  out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: br-knitr
#| include: false
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 11))
```

The figures use the helpers of @sec-gs, kept in the book's file `_figs-helpers.R`: a port of the
paper's plotting code, and `estimate_each()`, which runs independent targets in parallel processes.

```{r}
#| label: br-helpers
#| cache: false
#| file: _figs-helpers.R
```

## The data and the fit

`sc_example_data("br")` builds the paper's inputs from the bundled `br2017` data: the 1,991
respondents who answered the income question, 15,928 tasks, and 16 coded features. Plan A comes
first. Each rate enters utility through a linear and a quadratic term, and the revenue category
through four contrasts. The network sees age, sex, education, race, income and party ID, coded in
sixteen columns.

```{r}
#| label: br-data
x <- sc_example_data("br")
x
table(x$groups$party, useNA = "ifany")
```

The paper's party groups are Democrats (`party == "Dem"`, 885), Republicans (`party == "Rep"`,
643) and independents (`pid7 == 4`, 389). The 74 respondents who answered "not sure" belong to
`party == "Ind"` but to no party group, so the book selects independents by `pid7`.

The fit selected four taste factors. Reproducing it takes several hours:

```{r}
#| label: br-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:5, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
br <- sc_states(fit_q[[4]])                           # q = 4; M = 250 designs, 8 responses each
sc_save(br, file.path(fits, "br_q4.rds"))
```

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -4.865 | | |
| 2 | -4.796 | 0.0696 | 5.52 |
| 3 | -4.762 | 0.0337 | 3.76 |
| 4 (selected) | -4.742 | 0.0203 | 3.59 |
| 5 | -4.746 | -0.0047 | -0.75 |

## The recorded design

The displayed revenue category was generated from the six rates, with noise. A comparison that
raises one rate therefore also changes the revenue a plan is likely to show. The BR helpers handle
this, and they need the plans respondents actually saw. The function below takes them from
`br2017`, in the order of the fitted data.

```{r}
#| label: br-profiles
br_profiles <- function(ids) {
  b <- br2017[br2017$valid_income, ]
  b <- b[order(match(b$respondent, ids), b$task), ]
  plan <- function(k) {
    z <- b[b$profile == k, ]
    data.frame(tax_rate_1_pct = z$rate_L10, tax_rate_2_pct = z$rate_10_35,
               tax_rate_3_pct = z$rate_35_85, tax_rate_4_pct = z$rate_85_175,
               tax_rate_5_pct = z$rate_175_375, tax_rate_6_pct = z$rate_375P,
               taxrev = 3 - z$revenue_score)
  }
  list(A = plan(1), B = plan(2))
}
prof <- br_profiles(br$data$data$ids)
sapply(prof, nrow)
```

## Rate changes with revenue following the rule

For each bracket, the paper raises the rate from the bottom to the top of the bracket's menu (for
example from 5% to 55% for incomes above \$375,000). The other five rates average over the
contexts respondents saw, and the displayed revenue follows the experiment's revenue rule.
`sc_br_revenue_contrast()` returns that contrast as a vector of 16 coefficients. With `per_point =
TRUE` it divides by the change in the rate, so the mean is utility per percentage point.

```{r}
#| label: br-contrast
top <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
round(top, 4)
```

The rate part sits in `tax6_linear` (the quadratic term cancels because the menu's endpoints are
symmetric). The revenue part is the average change in the revenue codes that the raise causes.

```{r}
#| label: br-means
brackets <- c("under $10k", "$10-35k", "$35-85k", "$85-175k", "$175-375k", "over $375k")
contrast <- lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_br_revenue_contrast(j, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE))
means <- sc_estimate(br, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_mean(brackets[j], contrast[[j]])))
tab(means, 4)
```

Higher rates on the bottom three brackets lower utility on average, and higher rates on the top two
raise it. Per rate point, the penalty below \$10,000 is -0.0577 and the gain above \$375,000 is
0.0221. `sc_ratio()` compares the two, with a delta-method interval:

```{r}
#| label: br-ratio
ratio <- sc_ratio("bottom penalty / top gain", sc_mean("bottom", contrast[[1]]),
                  sc_mean("top", contrast[[6]]))
tab(sc_estimate(br, ratio))
```

The bottom-bracket penalty is 2.61 times the top-bracket gain.

## Preference shares

The share is the fraction of respondents whose utility change, averaged over contexts, is positive.
The paper's main figure reports it for all six brackets. Each share is a bounded update, so they
run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: br-shares
top_55_35 <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, high = 55, low = 35, profiles = prof)
shares <- estimate_each(br, c(
  lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_share(brackets[j], contrast[[j]])),
  list(sc_share("top rate 35% to 55%", top_55_35),
       sc_mean("top rate 35% to 55%: mean", top_55_35))))
tab(shares, 4)
```

An estimated 69.1% favor raising the top rate from 5% to 55%. For the \$10,000--\$35,000 bracket,
29.2% favor the higher rate despite its negative mean, and for \$85,000--\$175,000 the share is
54.7%. Raising the top rate from 35% to 55% splits respondents evenly: the share is 49.7% and the
mean is -0.013, with an interval that includes zero. Because utility has a quadratic term in each
rate, the direction of a taste can depend on where a change starts.

## Differences by party

The same contrasts by party use subgroup weights. A function of the groups returns them.

```{r}
#| label: br-party
party_w <- list(Democrats = function(g) g$party == "Dem", independents = function(g) g$pid7 == 4,
                Republicans = function(g) g$party == "Rep")
party_targets <- list()
for (j in c(1, 6)) for (p in names(party_w))
  party_targets[[length(party_targets) + 1]] <-
    sc_share(paste(brackets[j], p, sep = ", "), contrast[[j]], w = party_w[[p]])
party_shares <- estimate_each(br, party_targets)
tab(party_shares)
```

Among Democrats, 83.5% favor the higher top rate; among Republicans, 52.8%, with an interval that
includes 50%. Both groups largely oppose raising the lowest rate. In the figure, the lower row
shows the top bracket: the blue Democratic point sits well to the right of the red Republican one,
whose bar crosses the 50% line. The upper row shows the bottom bracket, where all three groups are
far below 50%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-party-shares
#| fig-cap: "Preference shares by party"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
paper_par()
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(2.15, 4.7), heights = c(3, .4))
row_labels(c("Below $10k", "Above $375k"))
panel(c(0, 100), 2, "Share favoring the higher rate (%)", seq(0, 100, 25))
for (k in 1:3)
  ci(pick(party_shares, paste(brackets[c(1, 6)], names(party_w)[k], sep = ", ")),
     2:1 + c(.16, 0, -.16)[k], color = cols[k], scale = 100)
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("Democrat", "Independent", "Republican"), col = cols, pch = 16, bty = "n",
       cex = .85, horiz = TRUE)
```

Bars are 95% log-odds intervals. The groups contain 885 Democrats, 389 independents and 643
Republicans, leaners included; the 74 respondents who answered "not sure" are in no party group.

The score correction matters here: before correction (the `plug_in` column) the top-rate shares
are 76.8% and 63.8%, a smaller gap. The difference between the two party means has its own
interval:

```{r}
#| label: br-gap
gap <- sc_difference("top rate: Democrats minus Republicans",
                     sc_mean("Democrats", contrast[[6]], w = party_w$Democrats),
                     sc_mean("Republicans", contrast[[6]], w = party_w$Republicans))
tab(sc_estimate(br, gap), 4)
```

## Fitted distributions

`sc_fitted_law()` gives the fitted law of each bracket contrast: for each held-out respondent, a
normal distribution of the utility change per rate point. The population law is their mixture.

```{r}
#| label: br-laws
laws <- lapply(contrast, function(cc) sc_fitted_law(br, cc))
bn <- c("Below $10k", "$10-35k", "$35-85k", "$85-175k", "$175-375k", "Above $375k")
```

The paper's appendix draws one panel per bracket. Take the first panel. The blue curve lies mostly
below the dashed line at zero and is wide: most respondents dislike a higher bottom rate, and they
differ a lot in how much. The red line marks the score-corrected mean, -0.0577, and the red bar its
95% interval. The last panel, the top bracket, is narrower and centered just above zero, with
about 30% of its mass below zero. As in @sec-gs, the curves are fitted laws before the score
correction, so a red line need not sit at a curve's center.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Fitted preferences over tax-rate changes"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.3
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(2.1, .8, 2.1, .5), oma = c(1, .2, .2, .2))
for (j in 1:6) small_density(laws[[j]], bn[j], pick(means, brackets[j]))
mtext("Utility per percentage point of tax rate", 1, outer = TRUE, line = .1)
```

The appendix also draws the tastes for the displayed revenue label, holding the rates fixed. The
revenue category (`taxrev`: 1 = much more revenue, 3 = about the same, 5 = much less) enters
through four Helmert columns, each scaled to mean square one; row `k` of `H` below is the coding of
category `k`. A contrast compares a category with "about the same". The rate coefficients are
zero.

```{r}
#| label: br-revenue-laws
H <- contr.helmert(5); H <- sweep(H, 2, sqrt(colSums(H^2) / 5), "/")
revenue_contrast <- function(k) setNames(c(rep(0, 12), H[k, ] - H[3, ]), br$data$data$feature_names)
revenue_laws <- lapply(c(5, 4, 2, 1), function(k) sc_fitted_law(br, revenue_contrast(k)))
```

The two curves for less revenue sit mostly below zero and the two for more revenue mostly above,
and all four are wide. These panels have no corrected means.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-revenue-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Fitted preferences over displayed revenue"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2, .8, 2.1, .5), oma = c(1, .2, .2, .2))
for (k in 1:4) small_density(revenue_laws[[k]], c("Much less revenue", "Less revenue",
                                                    "More revenue", "Much more revenue")[k])
mtext("Utility relative to about the same revenue", 1, outer = TRUE, line = .1)
```

## Complete tax plans

`sc_br_plan_contest()` compares two complete plans. Each plan's revenue category is drawn from the
revenue rule, so the contest averages over the categories the two plans could show. The paper uses
four plans:

| Plan | Under \$10k | \$10--35k | \$35--85k | \$85--175k | \$175--375k | Over \$375k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Progressive | 0 | 5 | 15 | 25 | 35 | 45 |
| Flat | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 |
| Status-quo analogue | 5 | 15 | 25 | 25 | 35 | 35 |
| Regressive | 25 | 25 | 15 | 15 | 5 | 5 |

The paper reports every pairing of the four plans, for all respondents and for each party group:
six pairs in four groups. The support for the second plan of a pair is one minus that of the
first, so the chunk adds the reversed rows.

```{r}
#| label: br-contests
rates <- rbind(progressive = c(0, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45), flat = rep(15, 6),
               status_quo = c(5, 15, 25, 25, 35, 35), regressive = c(25, 25, 15, 15, 5, 5))
groups <- c(list(all = NULL), party_w)
pairs <- t(combn(4, 2))
plan_targets <- list(); meta <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(pairs))) for (p in names(groups)) {
  a <- rownames(rates)[pairs[i, 1]]; b <- rownames(rates)[pairs[i, 2]]
  plan_targets[[length(plan_targets) + 1]] <-
    sc_br_plan_contest(paste(a, "vs", b, p, sep = ", "), rates[a, ], rates[b, ], w = groups[[p]])
  meta[[length(meta) + 1]] <- data.frame(plan = a, opponent = b, group = p)
}
plans <- sc_estimate(br, plan_targets)
support <- cbind(do.call(rbind, meta), plans[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")])
support <- rbind(support, transform(support, plan = opponent, opponent = plan, estimate = 1 - estimate,
                                    lower = 1 - upper, upper = 1 - lower))
progressive <- support[support$plan == "progressive", ]
wide <- round(100 * tapply(progressive$estimate, progressive[c("opponent", "group")], sum), 1)
wide[rownames(rates)[2:4], names(groups)]
```

The progressive plan receives an estimated 69.5% of expected support against the flat plan, 59.6%
against the status-quo analogue, and 81.0% against the regressive plan. Against the flat plan,
support is 79.3% among Democrats and 58.3% among Republicans. These contests set position effects
to zero and keep task shocks.

The figure draws the four schedules in Panel A and each plan's support against the other three in
Panels B to E. The top group of bars in Panel B is the progressive plan against the flat plan: 69.5%
among all respondents (dark grey), 79.3% among Democrats (blue) and 58.3% among Republicans (red).
Each bar's whisker is its 95% log-odds interval, and the dashed line marks 50%. The status-quo
analogue draws 65.1% against the flat plan, and the flat plan 82.6% against the regressive plan.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-contests
#| fig-cap: "Expected support for complete tax plans"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 8.8
paper_par()
par(ps = 12)
layout(matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6), 4, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(2.1, 3.05, 3.05, .6))
par(mar = c(3, 4, 2.3, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 6), ylim = c(0, 60), xlab = "Income bracket (lowest to highest)",
     ylab = "Tax rate (%)", axes = FALSE)
abline(h = seq(0, 60, 15), col = "#E8E8E8"); axis(1, at = 1:6); axis(2, at = seq(0, 60, 15))
title("A. Tax schedules", line = .8, cex.main = 1)
plan_cols <- c(blue, "#777777", green, red)
for (j in 1:4) lines(1:6, rates[j, ], col = plan_cols[j], lty = j, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topleft", c("Progressive", "Flat 15%", "Status quo", "Regressive"),
       col = plan_cols, lty = 1:4, lwd = 1.5, bty = "n", cex = .85, horiz = TRUE)
plan_labels <- c("Progressive", "Flat", "Status quo", "Regressive")
bar_cols <- c("#333333", cols)
for (j in 1:4) {
  opponents <- setdiff(1:4, j)
  par(mar = c(3.1, 6.2, 2.25, 1.1))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(.5, 3.5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "Expected support (%)", ylab = "")
  abline(v = seq(0, 100, 25), col = "#E8E8E8", lwd = .6)
  axis(1, at = seq(0, 100, 25), cex.axis = .9)
  axis(2, at = 3:1, labels = paste("vs.", plan_labels[opponents]), tick = FALSE, cex.axis = .9)
  title(paste0(LETTERS[j + 1L], ". ", plan_labels[j], " plan"), line = .65, cex.main = 1)
  for (k in 1:4) {
    z <- support[support$plan == rownames(rates)[j] & support$group == names(groups)[k], ]
    z <- z[match(rownames(rates)[opponents], z$opponent), ]
    y <- 3:1 + c(.27, .09, -.09, -.27)[k]
    rect(0, y - .07, 100 * z$estimate, y + .07, col = bar_cols[k], border = NA)
    for (h in 1:2) {                 # whiskers: a white halo, then a dark line
      ink <- c("white", "#111111")[h]; width <- c(2.2, .8)[h]
      segments(100 * z$lower, y, 100 * z$upper, y, col = ink, lwd = width)
      segments(100 * z$lower, y - .035, 100 * z$lower, y + .035, col = ink, lwd = width)
      segments(100 * z$upper, y - .035, 100 * z$upper, y + .035, col = ink, lwd = width)
    }
  }
  abline(v = 50, lty = 2, col = "#666666", lwd = .8)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("All respondents", "Democrat", "Independent", "Republican"),
       fill = bar_cols, border = NA, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = .9)
```

## Effects on choices

`sc_br_endpoint_ame()` gives the AME of moving one bracket's rate from the bottom to the top of
its menu, with the focal plan's revenue category redrawn from the rule and the opponent as
recorded. It integrates over both sides of all 15,928 recorded tasks, about 90,000 contest rows
per bracket, so each bracket takes about 20 minutes. The six brackets run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: br-ames
ames <- estimate_each(br, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_br_endpoint_ame(brackets[j], j, profiles = prof)),
                      cores = min(6L, parallel::detectCores()))
tab(ames)
```

Raising the bottom rate from 0% to 25% lowers a plan's expected support by 18.8 percentage points,
and raising the top rate from 5% to 55% raises it by 14.1 points.

The paper's main figure for this experiment puts the four views of each bracket side by side.
Read the last row, the top bracket. Panel A gives the mean utility per rate point, 0.0221, with
its interval. Panel B draws the fitted distribution of that taste, the last curve of the appendix
figure above. Panel C gives the share favoring the higher rate, 69.1%. Panel D gives the AME of the
full switch from 5% to 55%, 14.1 points. Panels A to C are per rate point; Panel D is for the
whole endpoint switch.

```{r}
#| label: fig-br-preferences
#| fig-cap: "Preferences over tax-rate changes with revenue following the rule"
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
yy <- 6:1; m <- c(2.8, .9, 4, 1)
paper_par()
layout(matrix(1:5, 1), widths = c(1.85, 1.6, 1.7, 1.6, 1.8))
row_labels(bn)
panel(c(-.08, .05), 6, "A. Mean utility\nper rate point", c(-.06, 0, .04), margins = m)
ci(pick(means, brackets), yy)
panel(c(-.3, .2), 6, "B. Fitted\npart-worths", c(-.3, 0, .2), margins = m)
for (j in 1:6) ridge(laws[[j]], yy[j], c(-.3, .2))
panel(c(0, 100), 6, "C. Share\nfavoring (%)", c(0, 50, 100), margins = m)
ci(pick(shares, brackets), yy, scale = 100)
ame_ticks <- pretty(range(0, 100 * ames$lower, 100 * ames$upper), n = 3)
panel(range(ame_ticks), 6, "D. Choice\neffect (pp)", ame_ticks, margins = m)
ci(pick(ames, brackets), yy, scale = 100)
```

Each contrast raises one bracket's rate across its menu, with revenue following the rule. Panel B's
curves are fitted values before the score correction, scaled to the same height. Intervals are 95%:
Wald for means and AMEs, log-odds for shares.

## Decisiveness of a swap

Decisiveness asks how often exchanging two plans' rates in one bracket would reverse the choice,
with the other rates, the displayed revenue and the task shock as recorded. `sc_decisiveness()`
takes each bracket's two coded columns and a menu: one row per rate on the bracket's menu, in the
same coding. The rate part of `sc_br_revenue_contrast()` with `follow_revenue = FALSE` gives each
row relative to the lowest rate. A common shift of the menu does not change the swaps.

```{r}
#| label: br-decisiveness
menu <- function(j, menu_rates) {
  cols <- paste0("tax", j, c("_linear", "_quadratic"))
  t(sapply(menu_rates, function(r)
    sc_br_revenue_contrast(j, r, menu_rates[1], profiles = prof, follow_revenue = FALSE)[cols]))
}
dec <- sc_estimate(br, sc_decisiveness(
  list(top = c("tax6_linear", "tax6_quadratic"), bottom = c("tax1_linear", "tax1_quadratic")),
  menus = list(top = menu(6, c(5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55)), bottom = menu(1, c(0, 5, 15, 25))),
  pairs = list(top = rbind(c(6L, 1L), c(6L, 4L)), bottom = rbind(c(4L, 1L))),
  names = c("top rate: 55 vs 5", "top rate: 55 vs 35", "bottom rate: 25 vs 0")))
tab(dec)
```

Exchanging top rates of 55% and 5% between two plans would reverse an estimated 45.4% of choices,
but exchanging 55% and 35% only 15.7%. Exchanging bottom rates of 25% and 0% would reverse 50.5%.
This took about eight minutes.

## The paper's full target list

The paper's main results file for this experiment has 43 rows: a mean and a share for each
bracket contrast, the bracket 1 and 6 contrasts by party, the 35% to 55% top-rate change (with
revenue following the rule and with revenue fixed), the 5% to 25% bottom-rate change, the twelve
plan contests, the ratio and the party difference. Written with the public functions:

```{r}
#| label: br-full
br_targets <- function(st, prof) {
  g <- st$data$groups; n <- st$data$data$n
  groups <- list(Dem = as.numeric(g$party == "Dem"), Ind = as.numeric(g$pid7 == 4),
                 Rep = as.numeric(g$party == "Rep"))
  party <- c(list(all = rep(1, n)), groups)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  add_mean_share <- function(name, c, w = NULL) {
    add(sc_mean(paste0(name, ".mean"), c, w)); add(sc_share(paste0(name, ".share"), c, w))
  }
  for (j in 1:6) {
    cc <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(j, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
    add_mean_share(paste0("bracket", j), cc)
    if (j %in% c(1L, 6L)) for (gg in names(groups)) add_mean_share(paste0("bracket", j, ".", gg), cc, groups[[gg]])
  }
  add_mean_share("top55v35", sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, 55, 35, prof))
  add(sc_mean("top55v35.fixed", sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, 55, 35, prof, follow_revenue = FALSE)))
  add_mean_share("bottom25v5", sc_br_revenue_contrast(1, 25, 5, prof))
  rates <- rbind(progressive = c(0, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45), flat = rep(15, 6),
                 sq = c(5, 15, 25, 25, 35, 35), reg = c(25, 25, 15, 15, 5, 5))
  for (alt in 2:4) for (gg in names(party))
    add(sc_br_plan_contest(paste0("contest.", rownames(rates)[alt], ".", gg), rates[1L, ], rates[alt, ],
                           w = party[[gg]]))
  c1 <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(1, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
  c6 <- sc_br_revenue_contrast(6, profiles = prof, per_point = TRUE)
  add(sc_ratio("ratio.bottom.top", sc_mean("bracket1.mean", c1), sc_mean("bracket6.mean", c6)))
  add(sc_difference("top.DemMinusRep", sc_mean("bracket6.Dem.mean", c6, groups$Dem),
                    sc_mean("bracket6.Rep.mean", c6, groups$Rep)))
  tl
}
```

`sc_estimate(br, br_targets(br, prof))` takes about eight minutes, most of it the bounded updates
of the 16 shares.
